articles.text: Piedmont Finance Director Michael Szczech Piedmont’s Finance Director Michael Szczech is preparing to retire from his position, with his last day on Thursday, January 23. A long-time resident of Piedmont, Szczech served as Finance Director for over seven years. As Finance Director, Szczech administers the City’s fiscal operations, including budgeting, investments, financial transaction processing, record-keeping and reporting, payroll, accounts payable and accounts receivable. He oversees a three-person staff in the Finance Department – City Accountant Ken Lee, Human Resources Administrator Stacy Jennings, and Administrative Services Technician Melisa Mariano-Reyes. Originally from Chicago, Szczech is a 27-year resident of Piedmont and has two daughters. He moved to California in 1989, motivated to move after visiting an uncle in the Bay Area during the winter. After enjoying 60-degree temperatures during his visit and then returning to Chicago where it was 10 degrees below zero, he decided it was time for a change and started looking for jobs. Szczech joined the city’s staff as Finance Director in July 2017 after a long career in the private sector. He came to the City from Café Press, a San Mateo-founded shopping company where he worked for 10 years as Vice President. Prior to Café Press, Szczech worked at Leapfrog, an educational software company based in Emeryville. Szczech was recruited to apply for the role of Finance Director by former Mayor Bob McBain, who pointed out the advantages of being able to walk a few blocks to work each day. After retiring, Szczech said he is looking forward to spending more time traveling, and has trips planned this spring to the Florida Keys and to Washington DC. Further ahead, he’s looking forward to his first trip to Asia, where he hopes to see Japan, Thailand, and Hong Kong. Szczech is pleased to be leaving the City in strong financial shape, noting that Piedmont has never used deficit spending in his time as Finance Director. He also lauds the Council for the fiscal discipline during the recent multi-year period of high transfer tax receipts. Unlike many neighboring cities, Piedmont never used these surpluses to fund day-to-day operations. Instead, these funds went to building up reserves and capital funds, allowing the City to invest in infrastructure. During his time with the City, Szczech is most proud of these accomplishments: • Implementing a new financial software system for the city in 2020, modernizing City practices and ending paper-based processes for accounts payable and payroll. • Establishing the PARS (Public Agency Retirement Services) Fund in 2018. By funding and actively managing this fund now, the City hopes to mitigate the impact of increased pension costs projected in future years. articles.text: Big crowd in fundraising event for Havens School The Havens Dads Club hosted their 17th annual Poker Night on Friday, January 10 at the Veterans Hall with 150 players enjoying an authentic Texas Hold-Em tournament. By the time Havens Dad Luke Schloegel won the final hand, over $62,300 had been raised for Havens Elementary School. “It started somber right at the beginning and then it became really fun and it reflected the motto of the ‘all-in for the kids.’ I did feel like people were all-in on it and that’s reflected in the re-buys,” said Havens Dad Babak Sanii who was in charge of the event’s financials, check-in booth and photography. The event allowed for eliminated players to buy back in, a feature which benefited Havens school to the tune of $30,000. Food at the tournament made it a challenge to keep the grease off the chips, as passed hors-d’oeuvres from Chef Robert Dorsey, a taco bar and multiple round of pizza deliveries from Arthur Mac’s fed the masses. Oakland United Brewing provided the suds with many beer options on tap. Coaches and Hampton Fields are closed for repairs and re-sodding until February 21, in preparation for the upcoming Spring sports and soccer season. The popular fields are closed every year in the winter to repair damaged turf, level out mud holes, re-seed grass, and aerate and re-sod the terrain for safety and quality of play. Depending on the weather, the germination of new seeds may vary. “If the weather cooperates, we get good results,” said Parks & Projects Manager Nancy Kent. “If the weather is super wet or cold, the seed doesn’t germinate as well or the sod doesn’t take hold as well.” While growing new grass and re-sodding the fields, people have to be kept off the field to allow the turf repairs to settle properly and new seeds to germinate. Taking advantage of the gap in outdoor youth sports in winter, the City uses December and January to make its repairs. “Ideally, we would be doing these renovations during warmer months, but that’s when everybody wants to use the field,” said Kent. At Hampton Park, the baseball outfield is fenced off to allow new seeds the chance to germinate. Both fields are scheduled to complete repairs and re-open by February 21. In fact, as a political science professor at the University of California, Berkeley, I regularly teach about such cases in my undergraduate and graduate courses. In such scenarios, the research tells us that people tend to underinvest in the positive action, in this case brush clearing and home hardening. A short walk around some of the hillier, more forested parts of our city reveals that Piedmont is no exception to this general rule: dead branches, fallen leaves, and even toppled tree trunks abound. I say this not to shame negligent homeowners – though research also suggests that a little shame can be an effective motivator in certain cases. On the contrary, it is entirely rational for a property owner to underinvest in clearing dried brush and flammable debris when they reason that the likelihood of their house burning down is just as, if not more, dependent on what their neighbors decide to do with their own yard detritus. This is precisely why such a case warrants government participation. Given that all of us in Piedmont jointly benefit when our neighbors invest in preparing their properties for fire season, it stands to reason that we should jointly contribute to the costs of that investment. I propose that Piedmont set up a small fund that can be distributed annually as an inducement to homeowners to clear dried brush and take other protective measures around their homes. This fund could be financed using existing city money earmarked for wildfire preparedness or using new money raised via a nominal tax on property owners. Homeowners in high-risk areas would receive priority for fund distributions, with remaining money allocated based on secondary risk. Notably, this money would not cover the full cost of home hardening but instead offer enough incentive to encourage homeowners to take steps they otherwise might not have taken. Small sums of money could be paid out annually for brush clearing activities, while larger grants could be distributed on a lottery basis, much like the statewide Earthquake Brace and Bolt Seismic retrofit program, which offers grants of up to $3,000 for home retrofitting. An initial pilot program could help Piedmont determine the minimum level of financial inducements needed to create results while also offering proof of concept. Moreover, none of this would be at the expense of other, more traditional means of community preparation. City staff are currently engaged in hazard mitigation planning. Given that, and given the saliency of the LA fires, there is no better time to encourage our local representatives to consider ambitious and creative solutions to wildfires. We risk everything by not bracing ourselves for the next fire. We cannot count on individuals alone to take the necessary preemptive steps to reduce wildfire spread. Let’s collectively invest in protecting our community from future disaster. Rebecca Perlman is a Piedmont resident and assistant professor of political science at the University of California, Berkeley. Her research focuses on the politics of regulation and climate change. articles.text: Piedmont City Council voted unanimously to approve the first reading of a new ordinance designed to stay on top of new state housing laws at their Monday, January 6, council meeting. The laws make changes to the approval process for accessory dwelling units (ADUs) and junior accessory dwelling units (JADUs), more commonly known as granny flats, in-law units, backyard cottages, garage/basement apartments, or secondary units. The recommended revisions to Piedmont’s ADU ordinance would make city code consistent with three recent state laws that went into effect on January 1, 2025. The laws governing the changes are Assembly Bill (AB) 2533, Senate Bill (SB) 1211 and AB 1332. AB 2533 legalizes all previously unpermitted ADUs and JADUs constructed before January 1, 2020. Permits for such ADUs/JADUs can only be denied if they fail to meet the required Health and Safety regulations. The newly legalized units will contribute toward housing production goals for the city, and Mayor Besty Anderson said she hopes that this step will help encourage community members with currently unpermitted ADUs and JADUs to acquire permits. SB 1211 allows uncovered parking spaces to be converted into ADU/JADUs and increases the maximum number of ADUs on a property to eight, as long as the number of ADUs is not higher than the amount of multi-family units. AB 1332 requires the City to create a system for pre-approved ADU design plans to be used by citizens seeking to build their own ADUs. Design plans would be submitted and approved by the City, after which citizens could pay a fee to use the already approved plans. When asked by the Council how these laws would affect the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan (the City’s plan to provide space for housing development in Moraga Canyon), Kevin Jackson stated that the City would be able to specify the number of ADUs that could be built in the development agreement with a potential housing developer. Piedmont’s Planning Commission recommended that the City Council adopt the proposed amendments to the zoning ordinance after a public hearing at their meeting on December 9, 2024. The Council will review the updates for approval at its January 21 council meeting. articles.text: At-risk Pittie mix Potpie is hoping the New Year will bring him a new home. Oakland Animal Services staff say this big boy of 70 pounds is big hearted and a true softie. He’s a playful, affectionate dog who loves to wiggle and bounce around with excitement and show off his silly side. He knows the all-important sit command, takes treats gently, and is working on leash manners. He would get on with a dog who matches his gentle play style, or as your one and only pooch. Potpie would be an affectionate companion and happily sit by your side for some love. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is seeking feedback from community members on proposed changes to business permitting on Grand and Highland Avenues. Residents can provide input on the proposed performance standards by completing a brief online survey that will remain open until January 20. The goal of the proposed changes is to streamline the permitting process for new businesses in Piedmont’s commercial areas. Currently, any new business wanting to open in Piedmont must go through public hearings before the Planning Commission and City Council in order to obtain a conditional use permit (CUP). The City’s Planning & Building Department have developed a proposed list of business types that would be permitted “by right,” meaning that they would be able to open in commercial areas without a public hearing process – as long as they conform to certain standards covering hours of operation, number of employees, and other limitations designed to ensure that new businesses are compatible with the surrounding neighborhood. The proposed standards would apply for future restaurants, cafes, hair salons, fitness studios, and other businesses along Grand and Highland Avenues and would apply only in areas already zoned for commercial and mixed-use activity. The initial proposed list of business types eligible for “by right” permits includes: • Food and beverage sales: Wine shops, Limited service restaurants and cafes, Bakery • Nurseries and garden supplies: Florist shops, Plant nurseries, Garden supply stores • Neighborhood serving retail: Clothing store, Art and Craft store, Book store, Bike shop, Hardware store • Office: Architecture, Engineering, Medical, Dental • Professional Services: Hair salons, Barber services, Yoga studio, Dance studio, Martial Arts studio, Photography studio, Tutoring Center • Other: Fitness center Businesses that do not fit into one of these categories would still be able to open in Piedmont, but they would need to go through a public hearing process and receive individual approval from the Planning Commission. These proposals were developed based on a series of Planning Commission and City Council study sessions in July-August 2024, as well as input from community members via an online survey conducted in summer 2024. New state housing law prompts code update for secondary units in Piedmont By Tony Simons Piedmont City Council voted unanimously to approve the first reading of a new ordinance designed to stay on top of new state housing laws at their Monday, January 6, council meeting. The laws make changes to the approval process for accessory dwelling units (ADUs) and junior accessory dwelling units (JADUs), more commonly known as granny flats, in-law units, backyard cottages, garage/basement apartments, or secondary units. The recommended revisions to Piedmont’s ADU ordinance would make city code consistent with three recent state laws that went into effect on January 1, 2025. The laws governing the changes are Assembly Bill (AB) 2533, Senate Bill (SB) 1211 and AB 1332. AB 2533 legalizes all previously unpermitted ADUs and JADUs constructed before January 1, 2020. Permits for such ADUs/JADUs can only be denied if they fail to meet the required Health and Safety regulations. The newly legalized units will contribute toward housing production goals for the city, and Mayor Besty Anderson said she hopes that this step will help encourage community members with currently unpermitted ADUs and JADUs to acquire permits. SB 1211 allows uncovered parking spaces to be converted into ADU/JADUs and increases the maximum number of ADUs on a property to eight, as long as the number of ADUs is not higher than the amount of multi-family units. AB 1332 requires the City to create a system for pre-approved ADU design plans to be used by citizens seeking to build their own ADUs. Design plans would be submitted and approved by the City, after which citizens could pay a fee to use the already approved plans. When asked by the Council how these laws would affect the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan (the City’s plan to provide space for housing development in Moraga Canyon), Kevin Jackson stated that the City would be able to specify the number of ADUs that could be built in the development agreement with a potential housing developer. Piedmont’s Planning Commission recommended that the City Council adopt the proposed amendments to the zoning ordinance after a public hearing at their meeting on December 9, 2024. articles.text: Piedmont’s Public Works Department completed a project to update signage and striping on San Carlos Avenue on December 20, 2024. The new signs and paint seek to make the divided street’s one-way roads safer and more clear. Public Works looked into the street’s signage after they were contacted by a community member, concerned that they saw a lot of people turn their cars down the wrong way of the one-way streets. The complaint was reviewed by a Traffic Safety Working Group composed of Piedmont police and public staff. The group meets once per month to review any complaints received and traffic incidents to find out if there is anything that can be done to make Piedmont streets safer. After reviewing the complaint, the Traffic Safety Working Group brought in a traffic engineering firm to assess the intersections and make recommendations. The City then implemented the firm’s recommendations, updating the street with a new “Keep Right” directional arrow sign and fresh paint spelling out “DO NOT ENTER” at the exits of the one-way avenue roads. These improvements are intended to improve traffic safety along Oakland, San Carlos, and Magnolia and reduce the number of wrong-way turns onto the oneway segments of San Carlos. “Whenever we receive traffic safety concerns from the public, we carefully vet the issues identified, evaluate our public spaces to ensure that we are following current standards and best practices, and if improvements are identified we look to implement them as soon as feasible,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “In this case, we believe that the signage and striping improvements on San Carlos Avenue will enhance safety for all users.” A new sign at the intersection of San Carlos and Oakland Avenues reads DO NOT ENTER.
articles.title: San Carlos Ave. receives new signage, striping

articles.text: Piedmont’s Public Works team responded to a report of a fallen tree on Moraga Avenue on Saturday evening, January 11. Dispatchers received a report about the tree at 5:30 p.m. on Saturday to which Public Works staff responded immediately. On Moraga Avenue, workers found a large eucalyptus blocking the road. It had fallen from the Mountain View Cemetery property. The tree was too large to be cleared with existing City equipment, so a contractor was brought in to help cut the tree into a manageable pieces. Working with the tree contractor they were able to clear the massive tree and reopen the road at 8:15 p.m., within three hours of the first report. A small number of properties lost power overnight due to the fallen eucalyptus, but PG&E was able to restore power to all homes by 6:30 a.m. Sunday morning. “Our Public Works crews consistently demonstrate their commitment to keeping Piedmont safe and clean, but no more so than during emergency events,” said Director of Public Works Daniel Gonzales. “Their responsiveness and diligence removing the fallen tree, cleaning the roadway and securing the nearby fence is appreciated by all of us.” Public Works uses equipment to clear Moraga Avenue after a fallen tree blocked the road. articles.text: At the January 8 school board meeting a second reading was held for a proposal of six new classes to be offered at Piedmont High School. Aside from AP Physics C, all the new classes are honors versions of existing Visual Arts and Performing Arts classes and will be offered next year. New classes of instruction, which grant an extra grade point, will now be offered for AP Physics C, and the Honors versions of: Acting, Jazz Band, Orchestra, Symphonic Band, and Dance. Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich and PHS Principal David Yoshihara gave the first reading on December 11 and again were on hand to further explain the courses, give data and discuss the impact upon students. “Do we have students say ‘I love the arts, I want to continue in the arts, but I’m not taking that next class, because I’m worried about my college apps’? Oh my lord, yes,” said faculty member Elise Marks. Marks called the decision to move away from favorite topics of study as heart breaking and quite common. The five new arts classes should help students avoid having to move away from their passions to take more AP and honors classes. “We already have students who are doing all these amazing extra things within the classes. They are teaching other students, student directing, they are already doing the work and getting no reward for it,” Marks added. AP Physics C will be calculus-based and for juniors and seniors. The course content will cover Mechanics and Electricity & Magnetism. Board members, teachers, students and community members concurred that the change would be beneficial. “Because these classes do exist within classes that already exist, they don’t impact our master schedule in any way. There really is no downside,” said Marks.
articles.title: 6 new Honors and AP classes approved

articles.text: Piedmont School District invites families to learn more about the Transitional Kindergarten (TK) program at an Information Night 7:00 p.m. this Thursday, January 16, at Beach Elementary School. TK blends preschool and readiness standards for kindergarten with a focus on hands-on and experiential learning. In 2025-26, children who turn five years old after September 2, 2025 and before September 1, 2026 are eligible for TK. TK is the first year of a two-year kindergarten program designed to meet the specific needs of four and five-year-old children. TK does not replicate preschool or kindergarten; it uses developmentally and age-appropriate practices. TK addresses the child’s language, literacy, and pre-math skills with an emphasis on social and emotional development and learning through inquiry and play. The TK program is taught by credentialed teachers with specialized training in early childhood. It runs five days a week. Children are enrolled in either an AM (8:20-11:45 a.m.) or PM (11:45 a.m.- 3:10 p.m.) session. TK offers a developmentally appropriate curriculum that allows students to explore, create, and learn through purposeful play-based activities. Social emotional, fine motor, and academic skills are all integrated in this hands-on program to build a strong foundation for kindergarten the following year. To read more about our TK program, please visit Piedmont. k12.ca.us/about/enrolling/enrolling-info

articles.text: On Sunday, January 12, the Oakland, Emeryville and Piedmont Girl Scouts kicked off the 2025 cookie season at St. Leo Catholic School with a Cookie Rally. Northern California Girl Scouts changed bakeries this year, so the event allowed girls to review continuing cookies, learn about new cookies and prepare for the season. Girl Scout volunteers hosted different stations to review all the skills the girls will need for success. At the rally, Girl Scouts practiced how to speak to customers, how to multiply and total orders, learned about vegan cookies, and cookies with peanuts. “It made me pretty excited for the start of cookie season, and now I want to sell 2,000 boxes of cookies,” said Brownie Winnie Pickavance. Thin Mints are back, but several cookies have different names and there are some new cookies in town. Cookie Season started January 13 and continues until March 16. Find cookie booths at ilovecookies.org. Cadette Charlotte Phung hands out this year’s cookies to younger Girl Scouts for taste testing and diligent review.

articles.text: The Wildwood Dads Club will host its 38th annual Crab Feed on Saturday, February 8, at the Veterans Hall. Tickets are still available for the celebration with unlimited crab, sides, beer and wine that runs from 6:00- 11:00 p.m. The fundraising event that benefits the 101-year-old Wildwood Elementary School involves dozens of volunteers and sponsors to put on the popular production which procures upwards of 250 pounds of crab for 150 guests. Co-leaders of the event are former Dads Club President Scott Zengel and Sergio Serna, and they aim to make the event accessible to every community member this year. “This year we lowered the price, because we wanted to attract as many people as possible who have never been to one,” said Serna. Purchase includes all-you-caneat fresh crab cooked two ways, oven-baked salmon, and sides like New Orleans spicy spinach, creamy mac ‘n cheese, Tunisian spiced corn, desserts, and coffee. Tickets include bottomless beer and wine, with specialty cocktails available for purchase at the bar. Live entertainment will be provided by Dads Club DJ Ben Anderson selecting the chunkiest tracks to wind up and close down the evening. This year’s theme is “Island Vibes,” so anything from a Hawaiian shirt to full-body porpoise or pirate costumes will be acceptable. “If your outfit conjures an island paradise, your favorite sea animal or the beach bum life you’re on the right track,” the dads state on their website. This is an adults-only event. Proceeds from the event will go to the Wildwood Dad’s Club to fund capital and infrastructure improvements to Wildwood Elementary School. The fun starts when doors open at 6:00 p.m. and the crab fest starts at 7:00 p.m. Visit Wildwooddadsclub.org/ crab-feed for more details of what promises to be an unforgettable evening of food, drinks, and festivities. Former Wildwood Dads Club president Scott Zengel dresses as Crab Daddy to promote the annual Crab Feed on February 8.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) for a fee. articles.text: It was a big week for Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team. On Saturday, January 11, the Highlanders claimed reversal of last year’s Div. 3 North Coast Section Championship loss to University, beating the Red Devils 82-79 in overtime at their home gym. Two days earlier, PHS beat San Leandro 49-39 at Binks Rawlings Gym in their first Western Alameda County Conference game of the season. Coach Ben Spencer feels their overtime win over University was among the best games of his six years at the school. “That was a top-five win in program history,” he said. ”We haven’t beaten them since the NCS semifinals in 2020 and we’ve never beaten them on the road. We were down 16 points in the third quarter,” Spencer said. It was a critical performance by senior guard Ravi Silverberg, who scored 28 points and had nine rebounds. Junior forward P.J. Brayer came up big with a double-double – 21 points and 13 rebounds. In the win over San Leandro, Piedmont had to work through some adversity after trailing 33-27 midway through the third quarter. With stout defense, PHS allowed just five points in the fourth quarter and six points in the final 12 minutes of action “It’s a product of young guys growing up. For a young team, it’s a great learning experience. I can think of missed plays where this could’ve been a 20-point win. I think we played four minutes of good basketball and it’s a 10-point win. If we play 10 minutes of good basketball, it could be 20,” Spencer said. articles.text: Gianluca Bini scored four goals against Encinal. Bosco Lorin had three goals in the 10-0 shutout of Encinal. Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team returned from winter break in a big way, toppling the Encinal Jets by a resounding 10-0 shutout victory under the lights at Witter Field on Friday, January 10. It put an end to a five-match winless run going back to December 5. “It was definitely a great way to start the year, it’s good to see the boys shake off the cobwebs. We still have to be relative; we’re going to have tougher challenges. But, it’s good for them to show success. We want to build on tactical concepts and adjust those concepts based on the opponent,” said coach Ben Russell. The brilliant offensive display featured two players gaining hat tricks with Gianluca Bini scoring four goals and Bosco Lorin with three. “It definitely build confidence for the team. Hopefully we can translate that to league against teams like Berkeley, Castro Valley, O’Dowd, and Alameda – those are going to be really tough games. Our discipline was lacking at the start of the season. If we can execute what we can do, I know we’re a really good team,” Bini said. “We’ve been lacking a lot in goal scoring and finishing. Getting this result is hopefully a good push in the right direction. The last couple of games we tied when we should’ve performed better. We went into this game knowing we had to compete and get a bunch of goals,” Lorin mentioned. Piedmont has a busy week ahead with three matches in seven days, visiting San Leandro tonight, January 15, then hosting Berkeley on January 17 and Castro Valley on January 21. Match Recap Piedmont led 5-0 at halftime and added another five goals in the second half. Their first goal was scored by Bini in the eighth minute after recovering a loose ball in the Jets’ penalty area, dribbling toward the net before slotting in a shot. Two minutes later, Henry Devan sent a perfect cross to Lorin running into the box, looping a well-placed header into the net. Then in the 15th minute, Bini scored again, this time sending in a laser after a ball fell to him around the top of the penalty area. Lorin made it 4-0 in the 25th minute, recovering a ball in the area to take a shot from close distance. Logan Faucher then made it 5-nil on a slick counter attack, where Niko Markopoulos sent a nice pass to Faucher running free in the box. Bini got his hat trick nine minutes into the second half, this time on a nice assist from Jacob Staff photos Henry Devan sends an assist to Bosco Lorin in the first half against the Jets. Rodriguez. Bini then scored his fourth goal on a shot from outside the box in the 59th. Lorin got his hat trick in the 63rd minute when holding off a defender to retain possession after receiving a ball over the top. Freshman Eli Dao-Hoang scored in the 70th minute when fellow freshman Russell Pan sent a slick low cross off of the end line to Doa-Hoang running at the near post. Sophomore Roman Ahearn scored via a free kick in the final minute of play on a shot about four yards above the penalty area. articles.text: Piedmont tied league rival Berkeley 1-1 on Thursday, January 9 at Witter Field, marking the first clash of the season between the WACC powers. It was a result that left coach Dan Chubbock feeling like they missed out on three points after going into halftime holding a 1-nil lead. “I’m happy with the performance, but we want to be winning these games. We’re at home and I don’t think Berkeley is as strong as they were in the past. We just couldn’t find the net, and I think we had enough to win,” Chubbock said. The Highlanders scored in the 29th minute when midfielder Juliana Thornborrow whipped in a low cross near the end line targeting Elsa Wallway, who made contact to redirect the pass toward the goal in close distance. It officially goes down as an owngoal on Berkeley, but Wallway’s shot was likely going into the net regardless. Berkeley tied the match with 19 minutes left in the game on a wellworked play, where a cross from the right wing set up a shot and rebound opportunity for the score. Despite dropping points, it’s a positive result given that Piedmont is without multiple defenders due to injuries. The injuries to the center back rotation allowed freshman Teah Suhr to step in as a starter. “I normally play a different position, but knowing we have injuries, I try to adjust to how we’re playing. The coaches are helping me play center back again and they’ve made things very easy,” Suhr said. Chubbock is also relying on freshman Ayla Blanford to get quality minutes on the wing, after getting minutes as a fullback in Thursday’s draw. “The injuries have been difficult; I’ve been playing outside back because we also have a lot of injuries there. But it’s been easy to adjust because our team is so nice and the coaches are really helping us,” Blanford said. The tie brings PHS’ record to 3-2-3 (W-T-L). articles.text: November 9. At Piedmont High, Smith helped the Highlanders win the 2023 D4 NCS title as a senior and claim back-to-back Western Alameda County Conference firstplace banners. She transferred to PHS as a junior after two years at Dublin. Basketball is proving to be one of the most successful sports at Piedmont High for kids intending to compete in college. articles.text: Award-winning flutist, bandleader, and composer Jamie Baum brings her quartet to SFJAZZ for the first time for two evening performances on Friday, January 24. Baum’s quartet will focus on the traditional jazz format of wind instrument with rhythm section and perform music ranging from Baum’s arrangements of both classic and modern jazz tunes. The flutist’s most recent recordings are a blending of South Asian, Near Eastern, and sacred Jewish traditions, with her newest release, What Times Are These, being the fifth with her expanded ensemble. Jamie Baum Baum was born into a musical family and attended the New England Conservatory of Music’s Third Stream program where she learned to master both jazz and classical music. Baum later said she was particularly fond of jazz music and graduated from the jazz department. She then received a master’s degree in jazz composition from the Manhattan School of Music. Baum studied under jazz multi-instrumentalist Jaki Byard at the New England Conservatory of Music, where she began the Yard Byard Project consisting of scores she received from him when she was a student. She founded the Jamie Baum Septet in 1999 with Ralph Alessi, George Colligan, and Jeff Hirshfield and has been an active flutist for over three decades. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse’s production of the hit musical Jesus Christ Superstar opens February 21 and will be performed on stage through March 30. The show features Deanalís Arocho Resto as Jesus and Sydney Jacobs Allen as Judas. Andrew Lloyd Webber’s rock opera recounts the final days of Jesus’ life and chronicles the relationship between him and key biblical figures, including Judas, Mary Magdalene and his disciples. The majority of the plot focuses on Judas, one of Jesus’ twelve apostles who is dissatisfied with the direction in which Jesus is steering his disciples. The musical opened on Broadway in October 1971 and was nominated for five Tony Awards including Best Score, despite opening to mixed reviews. “Jesus Christ Superstar tells the deeply passionate, personal stories of humans trying to love each other, battle their own demons, and falter in the face of their own grappling questions of what is true and right,” said Director Kimberly Dooley. Dooley added that she and the Berkeley Playhouse creative team see this show “as a movement opera, a sort of pulsing ball of energy and passion told through gesture and music.” “As we look into the kaleidoscope of the last seven days of Jesus’ life, we witness the hierarchies of power and politics juxtaposed against the radical love and compassion Christ represents,” she said. “We want to sweep the audience up with us and take them on this powerful visceral journey that explores radical love, the dangers of power, and the power of perspective.” Performances run Friday through Sunday and select weekday evenings from February 21 to March 30. To purchase tickets, call the box office at (510) 845-8542 x351 or visit berkeleyplayhouse.org. All performances at Berkeley Playhouse located at 2640 College Ave., Berkeley, CA 94704. articles.text: Join art historian Michael Stehr as he presents an illustrated lecture celebrating the art of Mary Cassatt, whose exhibit is now featured at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco. His illustrated lectured at the Piedmont Center for the Arts will be on Thursday evening, January 16 beginning at 7 p.m. ($20, cash only, at the door). The Impressionist movement of the late 19th century launched notable challenges to the art establishment in France. The bright, luminous renderings of contemporary life were a stark contrast to the highly finessed history paintings of the academic tradition. Not only were the canvases a stark departure from the status quo, but the roster of participants was as well. The Impressionist movement would be the first major revolution in Western Art that would have women playing a major role. One of these women, Mary Cassatt, would be the lone American participating in the movement. While overcoming great social obstacles, Cassatt offers substantial contributions celebrating the lives of women – both their work and their pastimes. While depicting images of work was nothing new, what was ground- breaking was the celebration of the work of women in the home, including child care, bringing a new-found focus to a labor that had previously been undervalued. Cassatt’s commitment to her subject was matched by her dedication to her trade. Bucking the expectations in her day of her class and gender, Cassatt was determined to be a professional artist; this was not a pastime, nor a hobby. Constant throughout her lifetime was her ambition and her devotion to work. Mary Cassatt’s “Mrs. Robert S. Cassatt, the Artist’s Mother” ca. 1889 ®
articles.title: Michael Stehr lecture at PCA on art of Mary Cassatt

articles.text: The largest and most comprehensive exhibition of American portraitist Amy Sherald’s work to date is on display at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) through March. Georgia-born Sherald is wellknown for her portrayal of prominent African American figures as intimate portraits. The exhibition, entitled American Sublime, features nearly 50 paintings made from 2007 to present, including iconic portraits of Breonna Taylor and former first lady Michelle Obama. In 2018, the artist was selected by the first lady to paint her portrait as an official commission for the National Portrait Gallery in Washington, D.C. Another highlight of the exhibition is For Love, and for Country (2022), which SFMOMA recently acquired for its permanent collection. “Amy Sherald is one of the most important artists working today and we are honored to present her first mid-career survey at SFMOMA,” Museum Director Christopher Bedford said. “Sherald’s vision deeply resonates with the museum’s goals to share and to champion a more expansive art history in our galleries. Her unique and exquisite renderings of her subjects encourage close looking, curiosity, and awe.” American Sublime is curated by Sarah Roberts, SFMOMA’s Head of Painting and Sculpture. “Sherald has invented an entirely new form of figurative painting. Her approach goes beyond portraiture to enact new conditions for seeing, feeling, and understanding shared humanity,” Roberts said. “In the spirit of great American artists like Edward Hopper, Alice Neel and Kerry James Marshall, Sherald’s works reframe our understanding of American culture.” Roberts added that Sherald’s portraits “invite viewers to recognize and move beyond preconceived ideas and engage in more expansive thinking about race, representation and the wide-open possibilities and complexities of every individual.” The exhibition will be on display through March 9. Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/amy-sherald-american-sublime/ to learn more.
articles.title: Amy Sherald exhibit at SFMOMA open until March

The 2025 fair brings together 59 exhibitors and 15 galleries participating for the first time this year, including Galerie Maria Wettergren (Paris), Herald St (London), Kiang Malingue (Hong Kong), Lisson Gallery (London), Peter Blum Gallery (New York), SIDE GALLERY (Barcelona), Southern Guild (Los Angeles), and Venus Over Manhattan (New York) in Pier 3, Charles Moffett Gallery (New York), Chris Sharp Gallery (Los Angeles), Fernberger (Los Angeles), François Ghebaly (Los Angeles), House of Seiko (San Francisco), Municipal Bonds (San Francisco), and Superhouse (New York). Sydney Blumenkranz joined the fair as its inaugural director this fall, after leading the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SFMOMA) events team for nearly six years. “FOG Design and Art has always been about celebrating our creative community and fostering connections within the art and design world,” Blumenkranz said. “I am honored to take on this role and look forward to finding new and impactful ways to push the fair in new directions, and to find more opportunities for engagement with the arts community regionally and around the world.” A special preview gala benefiting the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art will be held Wednesday, January 22. The preview gala provides support to SF MOMA’s exhibitions and education programs, which serves over 89,000 students, teachers, and families with online and in-person resources, programs, and visits each year. Food and beverages will be served and preview gala guests gain exclusive early access to the fair’s vast range of design objects, furniture, and fine art before it opens to the public the next day. articles.text: It’s become a genre unto itself: coming of age films that focus not on adolescents, but on those twenty-something boy-men who are grappling with and resisting the prospect of actually having to grow up. As if adulthood, and all it represents – responsibility, commitment, employment – should be, if not avoided, at least postponed. How long is never made clear. Adventureland is the antidote. It’s not a shallow knockoff, and it easily could have been. Set in a tacky amusement park, in 1987, spanning one summer, it might have wallowed in gratuitous, comedy-porn dialogue, seasoned with nonsensical slapstick. It doesn’t. It reaches for more. True, the film focuses on young people. But it does so with insight and sensitivity. It’s well written and wonderfully acted with a solid ensemble, each getting it just right. The setup finds one James Brennan (Jessie Eisenberg), just graduated from college, hoping to spend the summer in Europe, followed by grad school at Colombia in the fall. His plans are derailed when the family hits a financial rough patch. Instead of Europe, he ends up working at Adventureland, running one of the many game booths On his first day as a carney, James meets Em (Kristen Stewart), a student at NYU, attractive, enigmatic and seemingly out of Jesse Eisenberg and Kristen Stewart in Adventureland reach. With the introduction of Em, the film shifts focus, giving her equal time, and thus creating a much stronger and far more interesting movie from the standard guy-centric fare. From the first moment James and Em meet, it is clear that he is drawn to her. But this isn’t simply a courtship film wherein the guy pursues and then reports back to his buds, giving them way too much information. To its credit, Adventureland involves more than one focus allowing a number of characters to emerge, but never as caricatures. Each is interesting, and each has a story. Kristen Steward is a remarkable actress, recognizable from her early work in Twilight. She infuses Em with subtlety and nuance and all but steals the film from Jesse Eisenberg, so strong is her performance. Adventureland is a sweet film, satisfying and entertaining to the end. And don’t be mislead by the title. This is an adventure to be sure, but one of the heart. Adventureland. Written and directed by Greg Mottola. articles.text: Films such as The Karate Kid are unabashedly morality plays wherein the field of play is the context of choice. sports are so ideally suited to this predictable yet compelling narrative: adversity is confronted and overcome, the athlete prevails. The came cuts to scenes of cheers, raised arms, and gets ready for a warm glow. The wildly popular 80s martial arts classic of the same name, starring Pat Morita and Ralph Macchio, was set in Los Angeles. The more recent incarnation, released in 2010, takes place, interestingly enough, in Beijing and the sport is not karate but kung fu. Actually, it’s wushu, a more aggressive form of kung fu, involving punching and hard body contact. The template is familiar and the changes regarding geography and culture, when it comes to the core story, superficial. A young kid, Dre (Jaden Smith), from the streets of Detroit, arrives in China with his single mom, Sherry (Taraji P. Henson), who has a job with a car company. Dre is the new kid on the unfamiliar block and soon becomes the target of some local school bullies who are schooled by a cruel sensei in the art of kung fu. Dre’s life quickly becomes intolerable until he is rescued, literally, by the unassuming Mr. Han (Jackie Chan), the apartment building maintenance man, generally laconic, and yet deeply schooled in the martial arts, which he quickly makes obvious when Dre is attacked. Of course, there is a tween love interest, Mei Ying (Wen Wen Han), a gifted violinist, who befriends Dre. And so Dre’s training begins, including the familiar wax on, wax off, only involving a jacket. Jacket on, hang up, jacket off. Rinse and repeat. Dre is undisciplined and angry, wants to go home, and feels like a stranger in a strange land. He is, nevertheless, quietly and firmly instructed in the lessons of Kung Fu and, of course, in the lessons of life, all leading to the familiar climactic match where he meets his nemesis, Cheng, on the mat. The ending is foregone, the building tide of good feelings and anticipation are finalized with Dre performing a slo-mo kicking somersault that is the money moment in the film. articles.text: A pet column compiled by Piedmont pets Dear Abby: I ran into a cute Pomeranian named Shortbread the other day at Pet Food Ex and as I said hello and pet her, I noticed severe bald spots on her back. I asked her owner what they were and he said she had developed alopecia and had it for over a year. He said the only thing their Vet had said was to add a specific Fish Oil to her food. Afterwards, I wondered if it was infectious and if I could give it to my dog simply from petting that cutie Shortbread? Don’t worry. I washed my hands for two hours before touching Frank. –Jo and Frank the Tank Dear Jo and Frank the Tank, Alopecia, or hair loss, can occur with dogs due to a number of possible reasons: 1. Allergies: Dogs can be allergic to food, dust mites, mold, pollen, or other environmental factors. 2. Skin infections: Fungal infections like ringworm or yeast infections can cause hair loss. 3. Parasites: Fleas or mange mites can cause alopecia. 4. Diet: A lack of protein in a dog’s diet can lead to contracting alopecia. 5. Genetics: Some types of alopecia, like follicular dysplasia, are primarily genetic. 6. Hypothyroidism: This is the most common cause of non-inflammatory alopecia that appears symmetrically on a dog’s body. So yes, alopecia can be infectious but it’s unlikely. Often it develops from something in the dog’s makeup, an allergy or sensitivity to a particular food but be careful if you run into a dog that has it…I’m glad you washed your hands for two hours before petting Frank.

articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group tries to walk every Piedmont street each year, but in 2024 they didn’t get to the upper portion of Grand Avenue between Kingston and Greenbank Avenues. This roadway is well traveled by car, but not by foot, and the walkers know to really see a street you need to walk it. A large turnout of 56 walkers and three K-9 best friends were at the Exedra ready to go. The walkers went on Latham Street, the only Piedmont roadway named a “street.” There are only three houses on this oneblock street. They are long and narrow, built in 1960 and 1961 on right-of-way land that became available when the Key System C Line commuter trains to San Francisco were discontinued in 1958. The group went down Cambridge Way and over to Holly Place and its two houses, then to Lower Grand Avenue. The homes in this neighborhood were all built in the 1910s and 1920s. The group went up Lower Grand, came out on Arroyo Avenue, and went up to busy Pleasant Valley Road/Grand Avenue. A group photo was taken, and some roadway history was shared. As far back as the 1870s, today’s Grand Avenue was known as Pleasant Valley Road, which described the area well. It ran from Lake Merritt to the Piedmont hills. Today, the roadway in Piedmont is Grand Avenue until it crosses the Oakland city line where it goes back to being Pleasant Valley again. The group crossed the street at the stop light and made their way, three quarters of a mile, down Grand to the Piedmont/Oakland city line at Wildwood Avenue. On the way, they noted homes that were also built in the 1910s and 1920s, but were impressed by a new house with an ADU at its base that was completed around 2020. It was built on a lot that was long thought to be unbuildable. The group liked its modern design and construction. It is a large home, built with lots of concrete, up a steep incline. Architect Jim Kellogg said with all the concrete in its base it has nothing to worry about in an earthquake. The house is new, different, and beautiful. Jim liked it and so did the rest of the group. The walkers stopped at Grand and Linda Avenues where in 1892 there was a restaurant named “A Mon Chateau” (My Castle). It was built by Axel R. Gruggel. Over time, it had a number of owners and a trouble history with the City and police because of owner and patron behaviors which included no liquor licenses and gambling. In 1914 the building became the Grand Avenue Grocery Company and in 1922 the Del Monte Market. In the 1930’s Piggly Wiggly, as a division of Safeway, opened a second grocery store up the street at the corner of Sunnyside and Grand. It was stiff competition. The Del Monte Market floundered and closed, and the A Mon Chateau building was torn down. A series of gas stations later occupied the site. Finally, in 1987 the current, block-long Piedmont Financial Center was built there. Further down the street, some longtime Piedmonters remembered the site as a not-very-successful “Big T” grocery store, which eventually became today’s Ace Hardware, and a nearby hamburger restaurant. The group crossed Grand and noted that nothing much has been done to the former Shell gas station site since their visit last month. Someday it will be a Shell Recharge station. On the other side of Grand they could see an Oakland City Limits sign that confirmed they had walked the entire Piedmont length of Grand Ave. The walk had taken a little longer than usual, and it was time to climb back to the Exedra via Wildwood and Magnolia Avenues. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Wednesday Walkers gather for a photo on Grand Avenue on January 8. articles.text: It was a sunny afternoon on January 6th when the First Mondays Reading Group met for their first discussion of 2025. There was a big turnout of 24 readers The group was there to talk about A Farewell to Arms, a novel by American writer Ernest Hemingway, that was first published in 1929. The story is set during the Italian campaign of World War I and is a first-person account of Lieutenant Frederic Henry, an American serving as a volunteer lieutenant in the Italian army ambulance corps. The novel tells the story of Henry’s love affair with an English nurse, Catherine Barkley, and is divided into five sections, or “books,” that are narrated by Henry. A Farewell to Arms is considered an American classic and it established Hemingway as one of the greatest modern American writers. The book was his first best-seller and has been called the premier American war novel from World War I. The story has been adapted several times, initially for the stage in 1930, as films in 1932 and 1957, and as a three-part television miniseries in 1966. It had been a long time since many of the readers had read the book. For most it was in high school, and there were differing opinions about how well the book has held up over the decades. Hemingway was a great writer without question. He described situations in detail, but still allowed readers to create their own images in their minds. This ability to be descriptive but evocative at the same time, was recognized by the group to be a gift. Hemingway’s style was also innovative and broke the writing rules of his time. It worked then and continues to work now. As a child Hemingway loved Bach and classical music, and the melody of his prose – short sentences, and repetition – created a lyrical beat that engaged the readers. The group felt the book is a classic because it has great weight and importance in many ways. It is a love story set in a time of war. It also presented a view of life in a challenging time. While the readers didn’t contest Hemingway being a great writer, there were some members of the group who didn’t care for the book. It just didn’t play well for them today. It was shared that Hemingway wrote 47 different endings with 40 different chapter titles for the book. Many readers liked the ending Hemingway used, but others felt it was completely predictable and disappointing. Even more disappointing for some was the portrayal of Catherine Barkley’s adoring love for Henry. Her constant acceptance of anything associated with her “darling” was just too much for these readers. It was recognized that the book may be a period piece, but the dialogue still tired them. Some readers thought the book could be written and accepted today as a classic, but others didn’t. After the discussion was completed, it was noted that concern had been previously expressed that the group has grown so large and that having more participants might not allow everyone to share their thoughts. However, the 24 participants said that this was not the case in this discussion. They enjoyed the range of opinions and felt they were able to participate as they desired. The readers also agreed that A Farewell to Arms by Ernest Hemingway it is good for the group to read classics, like A Farewell to Arms, along with the contemporary fiction and non-fiction titles they usually select. This is a good mix that the readers enjoy and it expands their literary horizons. Future books The group had previously selected Endurance by Alfred Lansing for their February book and James by Percival Everett for March. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, January 15, 2025 First Mondays Reading Group explores Hemingway It was a sunny afternoon on January 6th when the First Mondays Reading Group met for their first discussion of 2025. There was a big turnout of 24 readers on hand. The group was there to talk about A Farewell to Arms, a novel by American writer Ernest Hemingway, that was first published in 1929. The story is set during the Italian campaign of World War I and is a first-person account of Lieutenant Frederic Henry, an American serving as a volunteer lieutenant in the Italian army ambulance corps. The novel tells the story of Henry’s love affair with an English nurse, Catherine Barkley, and is divided into five sections, or “books,” that are narrated by Henry. A Farewell to Arms is considered an American classic and it established Hemingway as one of the greatest modern American writers. The book was his first best-seller and has been called the premier American war novel from World War I. The story has been adapted several times, initially for the stage in 1930, as films in 1932 and 1957, and as a three-part television miniseries in 1966. It had been a long time since many of the readers had read the book. For most it was in high school, and there were differing opinions about how well the book has held up over the decades. Hemingway was a great writer without question. He described situations in detail, but still allowed readers to create their own images in their minds. This ability to be descriptive but evocative at the same time, was recognized by the group to be a gift. Hemingway’s style was also innovative and broke the writing rules of his time. It worked then and continues to work now. As a child Hemingway loved Bach and classical music, and the melody of his prose – short sentences, and repetition – created a lyrical beat that engaged the readers. The group felt the book is a classic because it has great weight and importance in many ways. It is a love story set in a time of war. It also presented a view of life in a challenging time. While the readers didn’t contest Hemingway being a great writer, there were some members of the group who didn’t care for the book. It just didn’t play well for them today. It was shared that Hemingway wrote 47 different endings with 40 different chapter titles for the book. Many readers liked the ending Hemingway used, but others felt it was completely predictable and disappointing. Even more disappointing for some was the portrayal of Catherine Barkley’s adoring love for Henry. Her constant acceptance of anything associated with her “darling” was just too much for these readers. It was recognized that the book may be a period piece, but the dialogue still tired them. Some readers thought the book could be written and accepted today as a classic, but others didn’t. After the discussion was completed, it was noted that concern had been previously expressed that the group has grown so large and that having more participants might not allow everyone to share their thoughts. However, the 24 participants said that this was not the case in this discussion. They enjoyed the range of opinions and felt they were able to participate as they desired. The readers also agreed that A Farewell to Arms by Ernest Hemingway it is good for the group to read classics, like A Farewell to Arms, along with the contemporary fiction and non-fiction titles they usually select. This is a good mix that the readers enjoy and it expands their literary horizons. pages.text: Wednesday, January 15, 2025 23 AMERICANS IN PARIS The Passion of Eugène Delacroix By Patricia Forsyth Privously printed in the Piedmont Post on March 2, 2022 The wood-frame home and studio of the painter Eugène Delacroix was purchased for preservation a century ago by the Foundation of the Delacroix Museum, and it remains a humble attraction at Place Fürstenberg on the Left Bank. The studio is a separate building behind the simply constructed, spare four-room residence, where the artist lived and worked on his final project – decorating the walls and ceilings of the nearby Church of SaintSulpice. This small museum’s collection consists of prints, writings, memorabilia, and minor oil paintings, takes about an hour to tour. But it’s not murals that Delacroix is remembered for, but the exhilarating, bold canvases he created as a young artist in his twenties and thirties. He was influenced by the great Théodore Gericault who painted Raft of the Medusa (1819). Gericault, only seven years his senior, was part of the Paris art commune; and Delacroix while still in art school posed as one of the corpses sliding off the raft. The artist worked alone in his various studios and died “without heir or pupil.” His works were sold off and scattered around the world. It is fortunate that the Louvre purchased Delacroix’s greatest paintings available for viewing in the permanent collection. Patricia Forsyth and Michael Mathews decamped to Paris as tourists in The City of Light. Comments to pkf.empower@ gmail.com. Galerie d’Apollon, ceiling murals by Delacroix. Louvre Musical Gourmet Continued from page 16 of yesteryear. Violinists of today actually exceed the perfection of Jascha Heifetz. I’ll tell you a little secret; if you listen to some of his recordings, there are places where he really messes up. But he actually wanted those to be included on his recordings. He was human. He had great integrity and sincerity, something I can personally confirm. Today’s players remind me of automatons. They are perfect today, yesterday and ditto tomorrow. Every performance is exactly the same. In the headlong quest for uniform perfection, however, they have lost their humanity. They make up for it with uniformity. Instead of looking within to their souls. We often read in the major newspapers that the musical performer “attacked the instrument”. Attacking the instrument is real big these days. So is “tearing into the instrument”. Loud is good, louder is better, some say. I am reminded of one of the great violinists of the past, Mischa Elman. When he was praised for his powerful tone, Elman always replied the same way: “the violin is not a trumpet. You say I have a big tone. That is only half the story. The other half is that I can play softer than anybody else.” It is that contrast which made Elman so marvelous. How important is nuance to art these days? Unique personalities and national differences made the old performers individual and unique. I much prefer that to the uniformity and predictability of today’s performers. Perfection they have. That is marvelous in its way. But the cost in humanity is lamentable. And so it goes in the world of music. Democracy is not a spectator sport! The world of high stakes poker is profoundly esoteric, and filled with inside baseball arcana, and the men seated around the table are distinct from one another in ways that are not self-evident, but sorted out by Molly as she balances on a high wire involving table stakes involving millions. Molly is, in effect, giving the film’s audience a master class in poker, her voice layered with backstory regarding those individuals who arrive at her weekly game, the buy-in just to take a chair is breathtaking. Keep in mind that the screenplay (the fulcrum being Molly’s arrest) and the voice over are written by Sorkin. Both are astonishingly good and demonstrate a kind of genius using language in an almost lyrical way giving the scenes a fullness that would otherwise be, well, beyond understanding (poker at this level can seem just beyond comprehension). I loved this movie, in large part due to Sorkin’s ability to write with an unyielding staccato style that asks a great deal of the audience. Viewing Molly through his lens we see Molly’s quick intelligence and resilience. She’s courageous, never risk averse, though the game of high stakes poker is always about unintended consequences. For Molly it’s also about integrity. Molly’s Game. Written and directed by Aaron Sorkin. Starring Jessica Chastain, Idris Elbas, Kevin Costner. 2 hrs., 21 min. Rated R. Released in 2018.
